title: The Foundations of ELT

pts: Every learner brings an L1, a purpose, and a starting proficiency — teaching begins with diagnosis, not delivery.
CEFR gives a shared six-point scale: A1–A2 basic, B1–B2 independent, C1–C2 proficient.
Needs analysis shapes syllabus choices: general English, EAP, ESP, exam prep.
points.who: Council of Europe (CEFR), Hymes' communicative competence

v: Outline of a human figure on A4 (see Appendix), coloured pencils or pens

items: Draw a simple outline of a person on the board. Choose a colour for each language you use and colour the part of the body where it ‘lives’ for you. Think aloud as you do it: ‘Kannada is my heart language, so it is red here. English is in my hands, because I write in English at work.’
Give each learner an outline. Ask them to choose one colour for every language or variety they know, even a little: languages they speak, read, hear in films or songs, or use with one person only.
Learners colour their portraits and make a key at the side. Allow ten to twelve minutes and circulate, asking gentle questions: ‘Who do you speak this with?’
In pairs, learners show their portraits using the frames on the board (see model language). At A1, let them explain in any language and use English for the key sentences only.
Collect the portraits. After class, tally the languages and note any learner purposes you heard. Keep the portraits: they are the first page of each learner’s profile (Unit 2).
With adults, add a second outline labelled ‘English in my life’, showing where they need English now and in the future (work, exams, travel, children’s homework).
With older teenagers, follow up with a short written paragraph, ‘The languages I live in’.
Support: provide the sentence frames on a slip of paper; accept drawing and pointing instead of speech.
Stretch: ask learners to add a ‘future colour’ for a language they want to learn, and to explain why in two sentences.

lines: This is ______. I use it with ______.
It is in my ______ because ______.
I want more English for ______.
S1: This is Tamil. I use it with my grandmother. It is in my ears because I listen to her stories.
S2: And this green one?
S1: English. It is in my hand because I write English at school.

blocks.x: What the portraits tell you, and what you might do with the information:

items: Languages learners share: plan which home language can support explanations and vocabulary work.
Purposes mentioned (films, cricket commentary, games, a cousin abroad): choose topics and texts.
Signs of confidence or anxiety about English: note for pairing and for Unit 22.

body: Purpose: to show learners what a finished portrait looks like before they begin. Content: a simple, friendly outline of a twelve-year-old figure, front view. The head is shaded blue (key: Kannada, ‘I think in it’); the heart red (Kannada, ‘my family’); the mouth green (English, ‘school’); both ears yellow (Hindi, ‘films and songs’); one hand purple (Urdu, ‘my neighbour’). A key sits to the right with five coloured squares and short labels in child-like handwriting. Style: clean line drawing, flat colours, no shading, suitable for photocopying in greyscale (use patterns as well as colours). Board version: stick figure with the words written on each body part.

items: Google Forms (free with a Google account). Build a short ‘About me’ form with five questions: languages used at home; languages used with friends; where you hear English outside school; one thing you want to do in English this year; how you feel about English (a five-face scale). Responses collect automatically in a spreadsheet, which makes the class tally in step 5 instant.

blocks.x: Give each learner an ‘About me’ slip with the same five questions. Collect the slips in an envelope, keep them in the register, and return them at the end of the term so learners can see how their answers have changed.

The Census of India 2011 recorded 121 languages spoken by ten thousand or more people each: the 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution and 99 others (Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India 2018). A class of forty in almost any Indian city is likely to contain more languages than a whole school in many other countries.

points.sub: The two halves of a language
pts: Skills: Listening, Speaking, Reading, Writing — receptive vs. productive, spoken vs. written.
Systems: Grammar, Vocabulary, Pronunciation, Discourse — the resources skills draw on.
Good lessons integrate both rather than teaching either in isolation.
points.who: Jeremy Harmer, "The Practice of English Language Teaching"

v: The story below (read aloud and one printed copy per pair); six simple pictures drawn on the board or on a handout

items: Draw or display six pictures in random order: a boy with a cricket bat, a ball flying over a wall, a garden with flowers, an old woman at a gate, a dog, a boy smiling with the ball.
Listening (gist). Read the story once. Ask one question: ‘Is the ending happy or sad?’
Listening (detail). Read it again. Learners number the pictures in story order.
Speaking. In pairs, learners retell the story using the numbered pictures. Do not correct during this stage; listen and note useful language.
Reading. Give out the printed story. Learners check their order and underline three past-tense verbs (grammar) and two words for places (vocabulary).
Writing. Each learner writes one new final sentence for the story.
Point to the board and ask: ‘When did we listen? Speak? Read? Write? Where did we look at grammar and at words?’ Label the stages together.
Replace the story with a local folk tale told in two or three minutes. Learners who know the tale in their home language can help with the retelling.
In a large class, run step 4 as ‘one sentence each’ around groups of six.
Support: give weaker pairs the first word of each retelling sentence.
Stretch: stronger learners retell from the point of view of the old woman or the dog.

lines: Ravi hit the ball hard. It flew over the wall into Mrs Rao’s garden. Ravi was worried. Mrs Rao had a big dog and a very beautiful garden. He walked slowly to her gate. The dog barked. Mrs Rao came out. ‘Is this your ball?’ she asked. ‘Yes, I’m sorry,’ said Ravi. ‘My flowers are fine,’ she said, and she smiled. ‘But next time, hit it to the other side!’ She gave him the ball, and the dog wagged its tail. Ravi laughed and ran back to his friends.
T: When you numbered the pictures, which skill was that?
Ss: Listening!
T: And when you found hit, flew, walked… skill or system?
S1: System. Grammar.

body: Purpose: to show that the four skills draw on the same four systems. Content: an outer ring divided into four quarters labelled Listening, Speaking, Reading, Writing. Two thin lines divide the ring into halves twice: ‘receptive / productive’ (left/right) and ‘spoken / written’ (top/bottom). The inner circle is divided into four segments labelled Grammar, Vocabulary, Pronunciation, Discourse, with small arrows from each segment to all four skills. Style: two-colour, clean, readable at A5; label text 10 pt minimum. Board version: two concentric circles with the eight words written in.

items: Vocaroo (free, browser-based, no account needed). Learners record their step 4 retelling on a phone and share the link with the teacher. The teacher can listen later and choose two or three short extracts, with permission, for a whole-class listening task in the next lesson.

blocks.x: Make it a listening task for the partner. While S1 retells, S2 holds the six pictures and ticks each one when it is mentioned. Then they swap.

body: Receptive before productive is a good default order. Learners who have heard and read language first have something to say when it is their turn to speak and write.

pts: English has 44 phonemes but only 26 letters — spelling misleads pronunciation.
Teach word stress, sentence stress, and connected speech early; they carry more meaning than individual sounds.
The IPA chart gives learners a tool to self-correct independently of a teacher's accent.
points.who: David Crystal, "How Language Works"; Adrian Underhill's phonemic chart

v: Word cards or a board list; four boxes drawn on the board labelled Oo, oO, Ooo, oOo

items: Say learners’ names and the name of your town, clapping once per syllable and clapping loudly on the stressed syllable: Ben-ga-LU-ru, KA-vya, ar-JUN. Ask the class to clap with you.
Introduce English words one at a time: teacher, banana, computer, pencil, hotel, photograph, eleven, tomato. The class claps each word before you write it.
Learners decide which box each word belongs in. Check together.
In pairs, learners find two more words from their textbook for each box.
Finish with one short phrase to show connected speech: a cup of tea. Say it slowly, then naturally, and let learners notice that of becomes a short /ə/ or disappears into /ə kʌpə ˈtiː/.
Use a ball: the learner holding it says a word; the class throws back the stress pattern in claps.
Older learners mark stress in their vocabulary notebooks with a small circle above the stressed syllable.
Support: work with two-syllable words only.
Stretch: introduce stress shift in word families: PHOtograph – phoTOgraphy – photoGRAphic.

blocks.x: A starter set of sounds and symbols for the phonemic chart (Unit 4 develops this):

lines: /iː/ as in sheep and /ɪ/ as in ship
/ʃ/ as in shop and /s/ as in sun
T: Listen: baNAna. Where is the big clap?
S1: Second.
T: Good. Say it with me.

body: Purpose: a board and poster reference for word stress. Content: four rectangles in a row, headed with circle patterns: large-small (Oo), small-large (oO), large-small-small (Ooo), small-large-small (oOo). Under each, two example words with the stressed syllable in capitals: TEACHer, PENcil; hoTEL, aGO; PHOtograph, CAMera; baNAna, toMAto. Style: the large circles filled, small circles outlined; readable from the back of a classroom when enlarged to A3. Board version: circles drawn with chalk.

items: YouGlish (free). Type a word and hear it spoken in many short video clips by different speakers. Use it to let learners hear stress in real speech and across accents; choose clips in advance for young learners.
Cambridge Dictionary online (free). Each entry has short UK and US audio recordings and phonemic transcriptions; useful for checking your own model.

blocks.x: You are the model. Say each word three times, slowly, then naturally. Ask learners to place a hand under the chin: the jaw drops further on the stressed syllable.

body: In Hindi, Kannada and many other Indian languages, a puff of air after a sound can change the meaning of a word. Hindi pal means ‘moment’ and phal means ‘fruit’. In English the same puff (aspiration) never changes meaning on its own, so learners from these languages already hear a difference that English ignores. This is a useful thing to point out when you teach English sounds: learners bring knowledge about sounds, not just gaps.

pts: Teach in lexical chunks and collocations ("make a decision"), not isolated words.
Frequency matters: the first 2,000 word families cover most everyday text.
Recycling and spaced retrieval beat one-off presentation for retention.
points.who: Michael Lewis, "The Lexical Approach"; Paul Nation's word-frequency research

v: The short text below on the board or a handout; coloured chalk or pens

items: Read the text aloud while learners follow.
Ask learners to find every verb that is followed by a noun: take a bus, make my bed, do my homework. They underline these ‘chunks’.
Draw a ‘collocation fork’ (Figure 1.4) for make, do and take on the board. Learners call out the chunks and you add them to the right fork.
In pairs, learners add one more chunk to each fork from their own lives.
Personalize: each learner writes three true sentences about their morning using chunks from the forks.
Next lesson, open with a three-minute ‘fork race’: call out a noun (a decision, the dishes, a photo); learners write the verb.
With young learners, mime the chunks and let the class guess.
With exam classes, add adverbs: make a big mistake, take a quick shower.
Support: provide the chunks jumbled; learners only sort them.
Stretch: learners find chunks in a page of their textbook and add them to a class ‘chunk wall’.

lines: Every morning I get up at six. I make my bed and have a quick bath. Then I have breakfast with my sister. At seven I take a bus to school. In the bus I do my homework if I didn’t finish it! School starts at eight. Our teacher always says, ‘Take your time and make a plan.’

blocks.x: A note on variety: both make a decision and take a decision are used by fluent speakers of English, and take a decision is common in British and Indian English. Teach both, and use the difference to show that collocation is about what speakers actually say, not about logic.

body: Purpose: to help learners store verbs and nouns together. Content: three large tuning-fork shapes drawn horizontally, the handle labelled with the verb (make, do, take), and four prongs each ending in a noun phrase (make: my bed, a mistake, friends, a plan; do: homework, the dishes, exercise, my best; take: a bus, a photo, a break, your time). Style: bold outlines, one colour per verb, lots of white space for learners to add prongs. Board version: a straight line with branches.

items: SkELL (Sketch Engine for Language Learning; free, no account). Type take and choose ‘Word sketch’ to see the nouns that most often follow it in a large collection of real English. Show this to learners as evidence, or use it yourself to check which chunks are worth teaching.
Quizlet (free basic version). Make a set with the verb on one side and the noun on the other; learners practise with the ‘Learn’ or ‘Match’ modes.

blocks.x: Keep a ‘chunk wall’: a sheet of chart paper on the classroom wall where learners add chunks they find. Review it for two minutes at the start of every third lesson.

pts: Present grammar through context and meaning first, form and rule second.
The PPP cycle — Presentation, Practice, Production — remains the reliable basic structure.
Focus on form should serve communication, not replace it.
points.who: Noam Chomsky's Universal Grammar; Michael Swan's "Practical English Usage"

v: A four-picture story drawn on the board; word cards for the verbs

items: Presentation through meaning. Tell a short story about yesterday using four board pictures: you waited at the bus stop, it rained, a friend stopped her scooter, she took you to school. Tell it naturally, with gesture, before writing anything.
Check meaning. Ask concept-checking questions (see model language) to confirm that learners understand the events are finished and in the past.
Notice form. Write the story sentences under the pictures. Learners find the verbs and sort them into two groups: -ed verbs (waited, rained, stopped) and others (took, came).
Controlled practice. Learners match verb cards to pictures, then take turns saying the sentences in pairs.
Freer production. In pairs, learners tell each other three things they did yesterday. Monitor, and note examples for feedback at the end.
Replace the bus stop with a local event learners know (a festival, a match, a wedding).
For a guided-discovery version (see Unit 6), give learners the sentences first and ask them to work out the rule.
Support: give the verb list; learners choose only.
Stretch: learners add a time phrase to each sentence (yesterday morning, at eight o’clock).

lines: T: Did I wait at the bus stop today?
Ss: No. Yesterday.
T: Am I at the bus stop now?
Ss: No.
T: So is this now, or finished?
Ss: Finished.

blocks.x: Learner sentence at the freer stage, with an error to note for later: I go to my uncle house yesterday → I went to my uncle’s house yesterday.

body: Purpose: to show ‘finished time’ visually. Content: a horizontal arrow from left to right. Near the right end, a vertical line labelled NOW. To the left, three crosses along the line with small labels: ‘waited’, ‘rained’, ‘took me to school’, and a bracket above them labelled ‘yesterday’. Style: simple, two-colour, arrowhead clear; suitable for the board. Board version: exactly as described, drawn with chalk in under a minute.

items: Google Slides or Canva for Education (both free for teachers). Build the four-picture story as four slides with one picture each; reveal the sentences on a click after learners have told the story themselves.

blocks.x: Stick-figure drawings on the board work as well as any slide, and learners enjoy guessing what a quick drawing shows. A rope stretched across the room with pegged cards (yesterday, now, tomorrow) makes a physical timeline learners can stand along.

pts: Reduce Teacher Talking Time (TTT); maximise Student Talking Time (STT).
Use Instruction-Checking Questions (ICQs) before every task, not after confusion appears.
Grade your own language to the learners' level without distorting natural English.
points.who: Penny Ur, "A Course in Language Teaching"

v: A ‘Find someone who…’ sheet (six questions such as ‘…likes mangoes?’); a watch or timer

items: Say it. Give the instructions in three short sentences: ‘Stand up. Ask your friends these questions. Write their names.’
Show it. Demonstrate with one confident learner: ask the first question, get an answer, write the name.
Check it. Ask instruction-checking questions before anyone moves (see model language).
Go. Start a timer for six minutes. Circulate and listen; do not interrupt conversations to correct.
Feedback. Ask a few learners what they found out. Note which questions caused difficulty.
After the lesson, estimate how long you spoke during the activity and how long learners spoke.
In a fixed-bench classroom, turn ‘stand and move’ into ‘ask the three people nearest you’.
For adults, use questions about work or family routines.
Support: pair a hesitant learner with a supportive partner for the whole activity.
Stretch: learners must ask one follow-up question for each ‘yes’ answer (‘Which mango do you like?’).

lines: T: Are you writing or speaking?
Ss: Speaking… and writing names.
T: Do you sit or stand?
Ss: Stand.
T: How many minutes?
Ss: Six.

blocks.x: Grading your language: compare ‘Now what I’d like you all to do, if you don’t mind, is to get up and move around…’ with ‘Stand up. Ask these questions.’ The second is not rude; it is clear.

body: Purpose: a small poster for the teacher’s desk. Content: four boxes left to right with simple icons: a speech bubble (‘Say it — short’), a person demonstrating (‘Show it’), a question mark (‘Check it — ICQs’), a green arrow (‘Go’). Style: bold icons, very little text, landscape A4. Board version: four words with arrows.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic version). Display a large countdown timer, a traffic light for noise level and the instructions as text on the projector at the same time.
Phone voice recorder (built in). Record ten minutes of your own lesson for the talk-time audit in step 6.

blocks.x: A sand timer, a hand signal for ‘stop and listen’ (one raised hand, class copies) and the instructions written in three numbered lines on the board.

body: Record ten minutes of any lesson on your phone. At home, time only your own voice with a stopwatch. Many teachers are surprised to find they talked for more than two-thirds of the time. Choose one activity next week where you aim to halve it, and record again.

pts: Distinguish errors (systematic, competence-based) from mistakes (slips, performance-based).
Delayed correction after fluency tasks; immediate correction during accuracy tasks.
Formative assessment guides the next lesson more than it grades the last one.
points.who: Stephen Krashen's Monitor Hypothesis; Merrill Swain's Output Hypothesis

v: Board divided into two columns; learners’ notebooks

items: During a fluency activity (such as the one in point 6), listen and write down four good examples and four errors you hear. Do not name the speakers.
After the activity, write the examples on the board in two columns: ‘Good language’ and ‘Fix it’.
Read the good examples aloud and say briefly why each is good.
In pairs, learners correct the ‘Fix it’ sentences. Check together, inviting self-correction first.
Each learner copies one corrected sentence into the back of their notebook under ‘My error log’.
With a confident class, ask learners to add a sentence of their own that uses the corrected form.
For writing, collect three anonymous sentences from homework in the same way.
Support: underline the part of each sentence that needs fixing.
Stretch: include one sentence that is correct and ask learners to find it.

blocks.x: Error or mistake? An error comes from something the learner does not yet know; a mistake is a slip in something they do know.

lines: Error (repeated, systematic): He go to school every day. She go to the market.
Mistake (self-corrected): She don’t — doesn’t like tea.

blocks.x: Board example after a speaking task:

lines: Good language: I went to my aunt’s house. (clear past form) / Me too! (natural response)
Fix it: I am liking cricket. / Yesterday we go to temple.

body: Purpose: to model a board layout for feedback after fluency work. Content: a blackboard divided by a vertical line. Left column headed with a tick and ‘Good language’, four sentences. Right column headed with a wrench icon and ‘Fix it’, four sentences with small gaps where learners write corrections. Style: chalk texture optional; clear handwriting font. Board version: as shown.

items: Padlet (free plan allows a small number of boards). Create a two-column board. After a speaking task, post the sentences; learners add corrections as anonymous notes from their phones.

blocks.x: Use the board exactly as in Figure 1.7. Keep the error-log pages in learners’ notebooks as the permanent record.

pts: Start every plan from a measurable aim, then choose activities that serve it.
Stage lessons with a logical arc: lead-in, presentation, practice, production, wrap-up.
Build in timing flexibility — a plan is a map, not a script.

v: 5 minutes at the end of a lesson
Board; small slips of paper or three coloured cards per learner

items: At the start of the lesson, write the aim on the board as a can-do statement: ‘Today I can ask and answer about yesterday.’
Refer back to it once during the lesson: ‘Remember our aim.’
In the last five minutes, learners write their name, the aim and one example sentence on a slip, and circle a face: ☺ ● ☹ (confident, not sure, need help).
Collect the slips at the door.
After class, sort them into three piles. The piles are your plan for the next lesson’s warmer and grouping.
In a very large class, use a show of fingers (three for confident, one for help) and count quickly.
With young learners, use a traffic-light card held up to the chest.
Support: give a sentence starter on the slip.
Stretch: learners write a question they still have.

blocks.x: A lesson plan in six lines:

lines: Aim: Learners can ask and answer about yesterday (A2).
Stages: warmer (5) – story and meaning check (10) – form (5) – controlled practice (10) – pairs speaking (10) – feedback and exit ticket (5).
Interaction: T–class, pairs, individual.
Materials: board pictures, verb cards.
Anticipated problem: irregular verbs. Solution: show the list; practise six only.
If time is short: cut controlled practice to 5 minutes. If time is left: learners write three sentences.

body: Purpose: a photocopiable planning sheet (Appendix). Content: an A4 portrait form with boxes for Class, Date, Level; a wide box ‘Aim: By the end, learners can…’; a table with columns Stage, Time, What the teacher does, What learners do, Interaction; two small boxes at the foot, ‘Anticipated problem and solution’ and ‘If time is short / long’. Style: clean ruled boxes, 10 pt labels, generous writing space. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free). A three-question exit ticket that learners fill in on a shared device or their own phones; results are sorted automatically.

Plickers (free basic version). Learners hold up printed cards; the teacher scans the room with one phone to record answers. Only the teacher needs a device, which suits large and low-resource classes.

blocks.x: Paper slips or traffic-light cards, as in the activity. Keep the slips for a week to see whether the ‘need help’ pile gets smaller.

dek: Unit 1 of 100: the groundwork every teacher needs before skills, fluency and theory build on top — from learner analysis to lesson-planning basics.

aims.x: This unit maps the ground that the rest of the book covers. It introduces the eight foundations of English language teaching and gives a first, practical taste of each, so that later units can go deeper without starting from nothing.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe the eight foundations and explain how they depend on one another;
gather basic information about your learners’ languages, purposes and levels;
distinguish the four skills from the four language systems when planning;
run one short activity for each foundation in a class of any size;
write a lesson aim as a can-do statement and check it at the end of a lesson.

why: Why start here. Every later poster in this series — fluency work, task-based learning, SLA theory — assumes these eight foundations are already in place. Skipping them is the most common cause of stalled learners.

background.x: Every language teacher, whatever the setting, is juggling the same handful of questions. Who is in front of me? What do they need English for? Which parts of the language should come first? How do I organize the room so that learners use the language rather than just hear about it? And how will I know whether any of it worked? This unit names eight answers to those questions and treats them as foundations, in the builder’s sense: they are not glamorous, and most of the time nobody sees them, but everything above them depends on their being there.

The foundations are not a sequence to be completed and left behind. A teacher planning tomorrow’s lesson uses all eight at once, in the same way that a speaker uses sounds, words and grammar at once. Separating them is a convenience for thinking and training, not a description of what happens in a classroom.

One idea connects them. In 1972 the anthropologist and linguist Dell Hymes argued that knowing a language means much more than knowing its grammar. It also means knowing when to speak, to whom, in what manner and to what end (Hymes 1972). He called this communicative competence, and the phrase has shaped language teaching ever since. It explains why this book begins with the learner rather than with the grammar book: the purpose of teaching English is to help particular people communicate in particular situations.

For many teachers in India, those people are multilingual before they walk into the English classroom. A child in Bengaluru may speak Kannada at home, Tamil with a grandparent, Hindi with friends and Dakhini Urdu at the shop. The National Education Policy 2020 asks schools to treat this richness as a foundation for learning, and recommends that the home language be used as the medium of instruction wherever possible until at least Grade 5 (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020: para. 4.11). English, in this picture, is an additional language that grows alongside the learner’s other languages, not a replacement for them. The activities in this unit and throughout the book assume that picture.

items: Learner profile check. By the end of the first two weeks, each learner should have a portrait and an ‘About me’ slip on file. Missing profiles are a sign of learners who may need individual attention.
Four-skills observation. During ‘One story, four skills’, use a class list with four columns and tick learners who complete each stage without help. Repeat with a new story after a month.
Stress and chunk quiz. A five-minute quiz: learners place ten words in stress boxes and complete five chunks. Mark together; keep scores for comparison later.
Exit-ticket trend. Count the ☺ ● ☹ slips over four lessons. A steady rise in ☺ against the same aim type is evidence that teaching is working; a flat line is a signal to change something.
Which of the eight foundations do you feel most confident about, and which do you tend to skip when time is short?
What do you actually know about the languages your learners use outside school? How could you find out more this month?
Think of your last lesson. How much of it was skills work and how much was systems work? Was the balance deliberate?
When a learner makes the same error again and again, do you treat it as an error or a mistake? How does that change what you do?
If an observer asked you for your lesson aim, could you state it as something learners can do?

terms.def: A description of what a learner can do in a language, as in the CEFR, used for setting goals, self-assessment and describing levels; for example, ‘I can write a short email inviting a friend.’
A group of words that is commonly used and stored as a single unit, such as by the way or Could you please…?; learning chunks supports fluency.
A combination of words that frequently occur together, such as make a decision or heavy rain; learners who know collocations sound more natural and fluent.

terms.term: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
terms.def: An international framework that describes language ability at six levels, from A1 to C2, using can-do descriptors; it is widely used for setting aims and describing levels.
The knowledge and ability needed to use language appropriately in real situations, including grammar, social appropriacy, discourse and strategy, not only grammatical correctness (Hymes 1972).
A short question that checks whether learners have understood the meaning of new language, such as ‘Is he still at school?’ after he used to go to school.
Natural, fluent speech in which sounds in neighbouring words change, link or disappear, as when want to becomes wanna; learners need practice in hearing it.

A systematic deviation from the target language that reflects a learner’s current knowledge, as distinct from a mistake, a slip the learner can correct. Errors show the learner’s developing system and are a natural part of learning.
Assessment used during learning to guide the next steps in teaching and learning, through questioning, observation, feedback and self- and peer assessment (Black and Wiliam 1998).
A short question that checks learners have understood what to do, such as ‘Are you writing or speaking?’ or ‘How many minutes do you have?’, rather than ‘Do you understand?’
An activity in which learners colour a body outline to show their languages and how they relate to them. It reveals the richness of learners’ linguistic repertoires (Busch 2012).
A performance slip that a learner could correct if asked, as opposed to an error, which reflects the learner’s current knowledge of the language and recurs systematically (Corder 1967).
A lesson sequence in which the teacher presents a language item, learners practise it in controlled activities, and then use it more freely in production.

The four language skills of listening, speaking, reading and writing, through which language is used. They are usually planned alongside, and distinguished from, the language systems of grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation and discourse.
The language systems of grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation and discourse, which underlie the four skills. Planning with both skills and systems in view helps teachers balance a lesson or unit.
The proportion of lesson time in which the teacher is speaking. Excessive TTT reduces learners’ practice, though well-judged teacher talk also provides valuable input.
The emphasis given to one syllable in a word, such as PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy and photoGRAPHic. Misplaced stress can affect intelligibility more than individual sounds.
